current_episode.title: Culture, Strategy and the Super App Shift with Nourhan Farhat

guest.titre: VP of People, Strategy and Ventures
guest.bio_context: Nourhan Farhat studied engineering before entering management consulting, spending 10 years in the field — including time at Roland Berger, which she credits as the first place she ever heard about consulting. She joined Kareem initially as Head of Corporate Strategy and Chief of Staff, before expanding her remit to cover People and Ventures. She describes her transition from consulting to the corporate world as driven by a desire to own deliverables and run a business with real P&L responsibility.

context.real_quote: Culture eats strategy for breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Strategies could be great on paper, but unless you really fix the operating model, the incentives, the entire culture of the company, the values of the company, I think that's the make it or break it.
key_stats: 10 years: duration of Nourhan Farhat's career in management consulting before joining Kareem
2012: year Kareem was founded by Mudassir and Magnus with the purpose of simplifying and improving people's lives
2019: year Kareem declared its internal 'Year of AI', embedding AI into demand prediction and dispatching systems before the current AI wave
4 years: duration Farhat has held the Head of People role at Kareem, originally intended as a temporary arrangement
Millions of captains employed and billions of dollars in earnings generated during Kareem's chapter one ride-hailing era, as stated by Farhat

I never loved any of them, to be super honest. I felt like it was a bit too repetitive for my liking. Consulting, I entered by a bit of a pure coincidence. And fun fact, it was Roland Berger's presentation that the first session that I had ever heard about consulting was Roland Berger giving a presentation about what consulting was and the typical... And I did find myself quite a lot in the consulting world. For quite a long period of time, the 10 years that I spent in consulting, I thought I'm going to just stay there. I really enjoyed it. I loved the problem-solving aspect of it and whatnot. And then another surprise came along the way where Kareem reached out for a corporate strategy role. I did interview, married that with a bit of... I did feel like a push to start doing things myself. Because in consulting, it's a bit more behind the scenes. You're inside the deck versus outside the deck. I wanted to own a bit more of the deliverables. So I said, you know what? Let me try to get into the business world myself. Max, I go back to my comfort zone of consulting. Four or five years later, I'm still in the corporate world and I'm quite enjoying it so far. Okay, great. And what did you say surprised you the most about that shift? As consultants, we feel like we're on the outside, but we feel like we're in the inside and that we know what it means to be an operator and to have skin in the game. I think it's a sentence that you usually say in consulting and it only really clicked. There was a light that sort of came over my mind when I joined the corporate world. We always used to say culture eats strategy for breakfast, right? I have seen it firsthand and now that I look, especially now that I look after both strategy and people, man, culture eats strategy for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, if you want. So you'll stand behind that? 100%. I think that's where strategies fail. Strategies could be great on paper, but unless you really fix the operating model, the incentives, the entire culture of the company, the values of the company, I think that's the make it or break it. Okay, great. Excellent. I'll incorporate that into my work. Yeah, we need to convince consultants it actually does matter. Yes, absolutely. I mean, at Arby, actually, I wear this hat of also managing the culture aspect, so I'm very happy to hear that this is also, you know, let's say permeating across other organizations. pending_qa.q: What is the 'culture eats strategy for breakfast' lesson Nourhan Farhat learned moving from consulting to Kareem?
pending_qa.r: Farhat says the phrase 'culture eats strategy for breakfast' was common in consulting circles but only truly clicked for her once she became an operator at Kareem. She now extends it to 'culture eats strategy for breakfast, lunch, and dinner,' arguing that strategies may be excellent on paper but will fail without fixing the operating model, incentives, and company values — which is precisely why she believes merging the People and Strategy functions makes structural sense.
